title: The earth
hookLine: Francis calls the earth sister and mother (Canticle of the Creatures)

cards: Brother Sun. Sister Moon. Brother Wind.
Sister Water. Brother Fire. That's the cast list of a short song by Francis of Assisi, the Canticle of the Creatures.
Tradition says he made it late in his life, when he was sick and his eyes were failing: a song in praise of the sun, from a man who could hardly see it.
He goes through the whole family of creation, one relative at a time. Then he reaches the ground under everyone's feet, and gives it two names at once.

teach.b: First, brother sun, sister water. In the Canticle, Francis praises God through each creature and gives each one a family name. The sun is a brother, beautiful and radiant.
Water is a sister, useful, humble, precious and pure. The singer stands among the creatures as kin, not above them as owner.

Second, our sister, mother earth. When Francis reaches the earth, one family word isn't enough. She's our sister, and our mother, who sustains us, governs us, and brings forth fruits and colored flowers and herbs.
Sister: kin, alongside us. Mother: she feeds us.

teach.h: TO DRESS IT AND TO KEEP IT.
teach.b: Third, to dress it and to keep it. Francis didn't invent this care. In Genesis, the first human is put in the garden of Eden with a job: "to dress it and to keep it."
Tend it and guard it. And the Psalms add whose it is: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof." In that picture, people are gardeners and keepers, not owners.
Fourth, heaven under our feet. Henry David Thoreau, in Walden, writing about a pond in winter, put it this way: "Heaven is under our feet as well as over our heads."
He wasn't a monk or a saint, but he arrived at a similar place: the ground is holy ground.
Sister earth isn't an abstraction. It's the strip of grass by the bus stop, the window box, the park with the litter in it. Love for the earth starts with one patch of it.

how: Christians sing and pray Francis's Canticle of the Creatures, and some churches and communities hold creation-care days, garden work and cleanups; Jews and Christians read Genesis 2 as a call to tend and keep the earth.

o: the lower world, far below the heaven above it
a resource people own and may use up as they like
the ground Francis called our sister and our mother

games.q: who said what about the earth — tap the pairs.
p: to dress it and to keep it

s: in the Canticle, Francis calls the earth both sister and mother
our sister, mother earth, who sustains and governs us.
in Genesis 2, the first human is put in the garden with nothing to do
the job is to dress it and to keep it.
Thoreau wrote that heaven is only over our heads
heaven is under our feet as well as over our heads.

games.q: you're the first human, placed in a garden that's not yours. what's your job?
o: use it up; it's all for you.
games.why: Genesis says the human is put in the garden to dress it and to keep it: a gardener and a keeper.

practice: Put your feet flat on the floor and feel your weight settle through them, down past the floor and the building to the soil, and rest your attention there for a few breaths.

Then let one patch of ground you pass often come to mind, a tree pit, a yard, a roadside strip, and see it clearly, litter and all, the way a keeper would. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for the earth beneath you.

wordCard.voice: The earth. The ground that Francis called our sister and our mother, that Genesis gives people to dress and keep, and that Thoreau found heaven in. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: sister earth. Kin under your feet, and a keeper's work in your hands. Day eight hundred sixty-six, done.
